figures.cap: graph of y=f(x): line segments and semicircle, 0 to 12

solutions.latex:
Add the signed areas between the graph and the $x$-axis (the semicircle has radius $2$; the area below the axis counts as negative):
$$\begin{aligned} 0\le x\le 4:&\quad 4\times3=12\\ 4\le x\le 8:&\quad 4\times3+\dfrac{1}{2}\pi(2)^2=12+2\pi\\ 8\le x\le 10:&\quad \dfrac{1}{2}\times2\times3=3\\ 10\le x\le 12:&\quad -\dfrac{1}{2}\times2\times3=-3\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{12} f(x)\,dx&=12+(12+2\pi)+3-3\\ &=24+2\pi\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
The diagram shows the graph of $y=2^{-x}$. Also shown on the diagram are the first 5 of an infinite number of rectangular strips of width 1 unit and height $y=2^{-x}$ for non-negative integer values of $x$. For example, the second rectangle shown has width 1 and height $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

\exfigure{268_q29_1}

The sum of the areas of the rectangles forms a geometric series.

Show that the limiting sum of this series is 2.
Use parts (a) and (b) to show that $e^{15}<2^{32}$.

solutions.latex:
Limiting sum $= 2^0 + 2^{-1} + 2^{-2} + \cdots$
$$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{a}{1 - r}, \qquad \text{where } a = 1 \text{ and } r = \dfrac{1}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{1 - \frac{1}{2}} \\ &= 2 \end{aligned}$$

criteria: Substitutes correctly into anti-derivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Limiting sum of rectangles $>$ area under curve between 0 and 4
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ \dfrac{15}{16\ln 2} &< 2 \\ \therefore\ 15 &< 32\ln 2 \\ \therefore\ 15 &< \ln\left(2^{32}\right) \\ \therefore\ e^{15} &< 2^{32} \end{aligned}$$

figures.cap: graph of the piecewise function: zero for |x| > h, peak 1 at x = 0, straight segments from -h to h
solution sketch: trapezium under f from 0 to h with parallel sides 1 and y, width h

parts.latex:
A function and its graph is displayed below, where $h$ is a positive constant.

\exfigure{1371_q10_1}

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}0&\text{for }x<-h\\[6pt]1-\left|\dfrac{x}{2}\right|&\text{for }-h\le x\le h\\[6pt]0&\text{for }x>h\end{cases}$$

If $\displaystyle\int_{-h}^{h}f(x)\,dx=2$, what is the value of $h$?

solutions.latex:
The graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis, so
$$\int_0^h f(x)\,dx=1$$
\exfigure{1371_q10_s1}

At $x=h$:
$$y=1-\left|\dfrac{h}{2}\right|=1-\dfrac{h}{2}$$
The region is a trapezium with parallel sides $1$ and $1-\dfrac{h}{2}$ and width $h$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}=\dfrac{h}{2}\left(1+1-\dfrac{h}{2}\right)&=1\\\dfrac{h}{2}\left(2-\dfrac{h}{2}\right)&=1\\h-\dfrac{h^2}{4}&=1\\4h-h^2&=4\\h^2-4h+4&=0\\(h-2)^2&=0\\h&=2\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
By using the graph below, which value of $k$ satisfies $\displaystyle\int_{-6}^{k} f(x)\,dx=0$?

\exfigure{317_q10_1}

solutions.latex:
$$\int_{-6}^{k}f(x)\,dx=0$$
Split at the $x$-intercept $x=2$ and at $x=4$; use triangle and rectangle areas, with areas below the $x$-axis negative:
$$\int_{-6}^{2}f(x)\,dx+\int_{2}^{4}f(x)\,dx+\int_{4}^{k}f(x)\,dx=0$$
$$\begin{aligned}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\times 8\times 5\right)-\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2\times 2\right)-2(k-4)&=0\\20-2-2k+8&=0\\26-2k&=0\\k&=13\end{aligned}$$
